it points to. Every reference has a lifetime, which is the span of code where it is valid. Usually the compiler infers it. When a function takes or returns references, it sometimes can't tell which input a returned reference came from, so you annotate it with names like 'a.

Annotations don't change how long anything lives. They describe relationships, such as "the returned reference is valid as long as both inputs are." The compiler then checks that every caller respects those relationships. This rules out dangling pointers at compile time, with no garbage collector.

- Returning a reference to a local variable: the value is dropped when the function
  ends, so the reference would dangle. Return an owned value (String, not &str) instead.
- Over-constraining with one lifetime: using a single 'a for unrelated inputs forces the
  shortest one on everything and can cause confusing "borrowed value does not live long
  enough" errors. Use separate lifetimes when the references really are independent.
- Structs holding references: a struct with a &str field needs a lifetime parameter
  (struct Parser<'a>), and it can't outlive its source. If that gets painful, owning the
  data (String) is often simpler.

fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
}
// The result is valid only while both `a` and `b` are.

● Lifetimes are how Rust's borrow checker makes sure a reference never outlives the data
  it points to. Every reference has a lifetime, which is the span of code where it is
  valid. Usually the compiler infers it. When a function takes or returns references, it
  sometimes can't tell which input a returned reference came from, so you annotate it with
  names like 'a.

  Annotations don't change how long anything lives. They describe relationships, such as
  "the returned reference is valid as long as both inputs are." The compiler then checks
  that every caller respects those relationships. This rules out dangling pointers at
  compile time, with no garbage collector.

  - Returning a reference to a local variable: the value is dropped when the function
    ends, so the reference would dangle. Return an owned value (String, not &str) instead.
  - Over-constraining with one lifetime: using a single 'a for unrelated inputs forces the
    shortest one on everything and can cause confusing "borrowed value does not live long
    enough" errors. Use separate lifetimes when the references really are independent.
  - Structs holding references: a struct with a &str field needs a lifetime parameter
    (struct Parser<'a>), and it can't outlive its source. If that gets painful, owning the
    data (String) is often simpler.

  fn longest<'a>(a: &'a str, b: &'a str) -> &'a str {
      if a.len() >= b.len() { a } else { b }
  }
  // The result is valid only while both `a` and `b` are.
